paragraphs: This paper investigates whether the speed at which a model learns can help explain which models should be preferred. Starting with linear models, it connects a measure of training speed to Bayesian marginal likelihood, a quantity used to assess how well a model accounts for observed data while averaging over its possible parameter values.

The connection has two consequences. First, the training-speed measure can estimate marginal likelihood, giving the learning process a role in model selection. Second, under certain conditions, the same measure predicts the relative weights assigned to models when their outputs are combined and trained using a regression loss. That second result concerns conditional behavior of model combinations, rather than a universal rule that faster learners receive greater weight.

The authors verify their results for linear models and the infinite-width limit of deep networks. Experiments with deep networks trained by stochastic gradient descent provide encouraging evidence for the same intuition. These findings suggest a possible route toward explaining generalization, while the strongest established connection remains in the analyzed settings.
neurips-2020-a-bayesian-perspective-on-t.tldr: A measure of training speed connects to Bayesian model selection in linear models, with encouraging evidence that the intuition extends to deep networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies pure exploration in linear bandits: how to allocate observations to identify a good choice, rather than maximize rewards during exploration. It considers both a fixed-confidence setting, where reliability is specified, and a fixed-budget setting, where the number of observations is limited. The challenge is especially demanding when the possible choices form a huge combinatorial collection.

Its central idea is to design experiments around the geometry of the choices. The authors use Gaussian width to define a sampling objective, drawing on methods that analyze the largest fluctuations across a collection of related quantities. This avoids an explicit union bound over every choice and differs from designs that minimize the worst individual variance.

A new lower bound establishes the importance of this geometric objective. The fixed-confidence algorithm matches that bound and remains computationally efficient for classes including paths, matchings, and matroids, even when choices are exponentially numerous. The fixed-budget algorithm has a guarantee matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, connecting practical sampling procedures to fundamental statistical requirements.
neurips-2020-an-empirical-process-approa.tldr: Geometry-based experimental design yields near-optimal exploration algorithms for linear bandits, including settings with exponentially many possible choices.

paragraphs: BRP-NAS addresses a practical difficulty in automated neural network design: evaluating candidate architectures is expensive, and simple estimates of hardware performance can be inaccurate. For deployment on a device, accuracy must be balanced against computational demands. Counting operations or adding measurements from individual layers can give an imperfect picture of how the whole network performs.

The method uses a graph convolutional network to predict architecture performance and guide hardware-aware search. It also investigates prediction across different metrics. To make better use of evaluated candidates, it considers binary relationships between models and an iterative strategy for selecting data. The aim is to improve search efficiency by learning useful comparisons and choosing informative evaluations.

The authors report outperforming prior methods on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201. They also find that the predictor learns useful features in the DARTS search space and improves upon its second-order baseline. Alongside the method, they release LatBench, containing latency measurements across a broad range of devices, emphasizing that accurate hardware prediction is itself an important part of architecture search.
neurips-2020-brp-nas-prediction-based-na.tldr: BRP-NAS uses graph-based performance prediction, model comparisons, and iterative data selection to improve hardware-aware neural architecture search.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates graph neural networks through their ability to count structural patterns. Such patterns matter in molecular, biological, and social graphs. It distinguishes ordinary subgraph counting from induced-subgraph counting: an induced match must also respect which connections are absent among the selected nodes. The distinction changes what a network needs to recognize.

The authors prove limits for message-passing networks, the 2-Weisfeiler-Lehman procedure, and 2-Invariant Graph Networks. These methods cannot perform induced counting of substructures with three or more nodes, although they can count star-shaped ordinary subgraphs. They also establish that 2-Weisfeiler-Lehman and 2-Invariant Graph Networks have equivalent power for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, and derive further positive results for higher-order methods and negative results for finite-iteration higher-order Weisfeiler-Lehman procedures.

Experiments support the theoretical findings for message-passing networks and 2-Invariant Graph Networks. Motivated by the counting problem, the authors introduce Local Relational Pooling, which performs effectively on substructure counting and competitively on molecular prediction. Together, the results make counting a concrete way to assess architecture capabilities and motivate alternative designs.
neurips-2020-can-graph-neural-networks-c.tldr: Substructure counting exposes provable limits of common graph networks and motivates Local Relational Pooling for richer structural prediction.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing builds a classifier by averaging predictions over Gaussian noise. This connects average behavior under noisy inputs to a guarantee against worst-case adversarial changes measured in l2 distance. The paper examines how to train the underlying classifier so that this smoothing procedure produces stronger certified robustness.

The proposed approach regularizes prediction consistency across noise realizations. In plain terms, training encourages the classifier to respond similarly when different Gaussian disturbances are applied to an input. The authors find that this consistency strongly influences the trade-off between ordinary accuracy and certified robustness. They use the relationship to construct a robust training objective without relying on a soft approximation of the smoothed classifier.

Experiments across multiple network architectures and datasets show substantial improvements in certified l2 robustness. The method achieves results better than or comparable to the evaluated state-of-the-art approaches while requiring significantly less training cost and fewer hyperparameters. The contribution is a training principle: making predictions agree under noise can improve the robustness guarantees obtained through smoothing.
neurips-2020-consistency-regularization-.tldr: Encouraging consistent predictions under Gaussian noise improves the certified robustness of smoothed classifiers with comparatively low training cost.

paragraphs: Deep Shells tackles correspondence between three-dimensional shapes: determining which locations on one surface match locations on another. It builds on smooth shells, a correspondence method that requires a stochastic search over initial poses before matching. The paper aims to replace that expensive preprocessing with initializations learned directly from the input surfaces.

The authors derive a hierarchical, fully differentiable matching procedure using entropy-regularized optimal transport. Its multiscale structure becomes part of a neural network, allowing matching and learned features to work together. A local feature extractor uses smooth, truncated spectral convolution filters. Because the matching pipeline is differentiable, it can be combined with this feature extractor within the proposed unsupervised learning approach.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over existing methods on multiple datasets, including comparisons with recent supervised approaches. The authors also apply the learned filters to shapes that differ substantially from the training examples and report strong generalization. These findings support learning the initialization and matching features as a way to improve correspondence without supervised training.
neurips-2020-deep-shells-unsupervised-sh.tldr: Deep Shells learns unsupervised 3D shape matching through a differentiable optimal-transport pipeline that replaces costly initialization search.

paragraphs: Data augmentation commonly teaches a classifier to assign the same label to slightly altered versions of an input. Deep subspace clustering cannot use that instruction directly because it lacks ground-truth labels. This paper instead asks the learned representation to preserve its subspace structure when inputs undergo small transformations, adapting the consistency idea to an unsupervised task.

The method adds a temporal ensembling component to the clustering objective. This encourages consistent subspaces across randomly transformed inputs, providing a training signal without labeled categories. The authors also propose an unsupervised procedure for choosing augmentation policies. Each policy specifies an image transformation, its strength, and the probability that it is applied during an epoch.

To select a policy, the procedure searches common augmentation choices and favors the one yielding the highest mean Silhouette coefficient on the target dataset. This uses the structure of the resulting clusters to guide augmentation selection. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on four standard subspace clustering datasets, supporting both the consistency objective and the practical value of selecting augmentations without labels.
neurips-2020-deep-subspace-clustering-wi.tldr: Subspace consistency and unsupervised augmentation selection bring the benefits of transformed training inputs to deep subspace clustering.

paragraphs: Estimating a neural network's uncertainty often requires evaluating it several times, which can be costly when computation is limited. This paper makes network depth the object of probabilistic reasoning. Rather than committing to a single depth, it considers different depths as alternative subnetworks whose predictions contribute to the final answer.

These subnetworks share weights, and their outputs are combined by marginalizing over depth. The sequential structure of a feed-forward network makes this efficient: reaching deeper layers already involves computing the earlier ones. The method exploits that shared computation to evaluate its training objective and produce predictions using one forward pass. Uncertainty therefore comes from combining depth alternatives within a single network evaluation.

The authors test the approach on real-world regression and image classification tasks. They report uncertainty calibration, robustness under dataset shift, and accuracy competitive with more computationally expensive baselines. The findings show that, in the evaluated settings, reasoning over depth offers a practical way to obtain useful model uncertainty while keeping the number of forward passes low.
neurips-2020-depth-uncertainty-in-neural.tldr: Probabilistically combining shared-weight subnetworks of different depths provides useful uncertainty estimates in a single forward pass.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to evaluate and improve a deterministic policy using data collected by a different, fixed behavior policy. Actions are continuous, and the target policy selects one specific action for each state. This offline setting matters when collecting new experimental data is constrained, because policy learning must depend on previously logged experience.

A central obstacle is that standard importance-sampling and doubly robust estimators require a density ratio that does not exist in this setting. Consequently, those usual value and gradient estimators cannot be applied directly. The authors develop several new doubly robust estimators using different kernelization approaches, introducing a way to handle the mismatch created by deterministic target actions.

The paper analyzes each estimator's asymptotic mean-squared error under mild conditions on the convergence rates of auxiliary, or nuisance, estimators. It also shows how to obtain a rate that does not depend on horizon length. This result concerns the estimation rate under the stated conditions, providing a theoretical route to evaluating deterministic policies without a rate that worsens with longer horizons.
neurips-2020-doubly-robust-off-policy-va.tldr: Kernel-based doubly robust estimators enable off-policy value and gradient estimation for deterministic continuous-action policies, with a horizon-independent rate under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Optimal transport studies how to move mass between distributions. Adding entropy regularization makes numerical computation useful across many applications, but explicit formulas have been scarce. This paper derives a closed-form solution for entropy-regularized transport between Gaussian measures, connecting a widely used computational approach with an analytically tractable family.

The derivation solves the fixed-point equation underlying Sinkhorn's algorithm. The resulting expression is differentiable everywhere, including when Gaussian covariance matrices are degenerate. This differentiability distinguishes it from the unregularized Wasserstein-Bures expression discussed by the authors. The work also identifies the optimal transport plans as Gaussian and gives formulas for their parameters, describing both the transport cost and the matching of mass.

The method extends to unbalanced measures, where Gaussians are multiplied by positive constants and need not have equal total mass. Its formulas expose the trade-off between transporting mass and destroying it. In both balanced and unbalanced settings, the analytical solutions provide ground truth for studying entropy-regularized transport and the behavior of Sinkhorn's algorithm.
neurips-2020-entropic-optimal-transport-.tldr: The paper derives differentiable closed-form solutions and optimal plans for entropy-regularized transport between balanced and unbalanced Gaussian measures.

paragraphs: The paper brings together two perspectives on communication between learning agents. Emergent language concerns how a communication system develops through repeated training. Pragmatic reasoning concerns how agents interpret and choose messages in a particular interaction while considering one another. These processes operate on different timescales, but both can influence whether a message succeeds.

The authors combine computational models of short-term mutual reasoning with long-term language emergence. In the reinforcement-learning view used here, the long-term process involves stochastic games and reinforcement training, while pragmatic interaction involves stage games with awareness of the other agent. The combination lets communication be shaped both by accumulated learning and by reasoning about the current partner.

The study examines referential games and StarCraft II, comparing different mutual-reasoning models through empirical and theoretical analysis. The results highlight the relevance of pragmatics for progress toward communication that is more natural, accurate, robust, detailed, and concise. The contribution is evidence about the relative merits of these reasoning models, supporting their role in improving emergent language.
neurips-2020-incorporating-pragmatic-rea.tldr: Combining immediate reasoning about communication partners with long-term language learning offers a promising route toward better agent utterances.

paragraphs: Gradient-based architecture search often trains a dense network containing many candidate connections, then removes connections to obtain the final architecture. This creates both training expense and a mismatch between the network searched and the network evaluated. ISTA-NAS treats sparsity as part of the search problem itself, rather than introducing it only through post-processing.

The method formulates architecture search as sparse coding. Differentiable optimization takes place in a compressed space with the same validation loss as the original sparse solution space, alternating with sparse architecture recovery. The search network therefore satisfies the sparsity constraint at every update. A further one-stage method uses the target network's depth and width during search, then absorbs architecture variables into its weights.

The authors report a search cost of 0.05 GPU-day for their two-stage method on CIFAR-10. Their one-stage approach obtains state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet at the cost of evaluation training alone. The approach delivers architecture and trained parameters together while addressing both connection sparsity and differences in network dimensions.
neurips-2020-ista-nas-efficient-and-cons.tldr: ISTA-NAS uses sparse coding to keep architecture search sparse and can jointly produce an architecture and trained weights in one run.

paragraphs: Modeling discrete structures involves a tension between flexibility and manageable computation. Autoregressive models provide a tractable approach, while energy-based models offer more flexibility but require estimating a partition function. This paper develops a learning algorithm for both conditional and unconditional energy-based models of discrete structured data, with applications including software-related tasks.

The algorithm estimates parameter gradients using a learned sampler that imitates local search. Rather than treating sampling as a separate fixed procedure, it learns the sampler alongside the energy function. A new variational formulation of power iteration enables efficient training of both components. This connects the model's expressive scoring mechanism with a trainable method for exploring discrete possibilities.

The authors report significant improvements from learning local search in challenging application domains. A prominent example is a software-testing fuzzer guided by an energy model, which achieves performance comparable to carefully engineered engines such as libFuzzer. The results support the proposed balance between modeling flexibility and computational tractability, including a practical use beyond prediction alone.
neurips-2020-learning-discrete-energy-ba.tldr: A jointly learned local-search sampler makes discrete energy-based model training practical and supports competitive energy-guided software fuzzing.

paragraphs: In one-shot video object segmentation, the first mask of each object is supplied at test time, and the system must segment that object throughout the video. Adapting a model to the supplied mask can help, but the resulting test-time training has been considered too slow. This paper introduces e-OSVOS to make that adaptation more efficient.

The method separates object detection from segmentation and uses a modified Mask R-CNN to predict local masks. It meta-learns both the model's starting parameters and its learning rates for test-time optimization, including individual rates at the neuron level. This replaces a laborious manual search for adaptation settings with learned choices intended to improve runtime and performance together.

To address degradation as a video progresses, the model continues adapting using earlier mask predictions, supported by bounding-box propagation between frames. The authors report state-of-the-art results among one-shot fine-tuning methods on DAVIS 2016, DAVIS 2017, and YouTube-VOS, alongside substantially reduced test runtime. The findings support revisiting test-time optimization when its initialization and update behavior are explicitly learned.
neurips-2020-make-one-shot-video-object-.tldr: e-OSVOS makes one-shot video segmentation faster through learned adaptation settings, local mask prediction, and continued adaptation across frames.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose among learning algorithms while interacting with a stochastic bandit environment. A master algorithm selects between candidate base algorithms, allowing model selection to happen during learning. The authors develop an abstraction that accommodates general base algorithms and different adversarial master algorithms, rather than requiring one particular pairing.

A generic smoothing transformation enables an optimal regret guarantee growing as the square root of the number of rounds, provided the optimal base algorithm has a high-probability regret guarantee. A matching lower bound shows that this square-root cost is unavoidable in general, even when one candidate alone would achieve logarithmic regret. Selecting a good learner can therefore be fundamentally harder than running it with advance knowledge.

The framework applies to misspecified linear contextual bandits, unknown linear dimension, and reinforcement learning with unknown feature maps. A consequential requirement is that the proposed algorithm needs the optimal base regret to set the master's learning rate. The authors also show that, without this prior knowledge, any master can incur regret exceeding that of the optimal base.
neurips-2020-model-selection-in-contextu.tldr: A smoothing-based master algorithm achieves optimal square-root bandit model-selection regret under stated guarantees and knowledge of the optimal base regret.

paragraphs: The paper compares two ways to make an input specify a function. An embedding-based system encodes the input and feeds that code into a fixed network alongside the function's argument. A hypernetwork instead generates the weights of a network that implements the desired function. The authors define modularity as the ability to effectively learn a different function for each input instance.

They study this property through expressivity and parameter complexity. Their theoretical development supplies a lower bound on the number of trainable parameters needed for function approximation while removing a robustness requirement from earlier approximation theory. They then use the bound to compare the network receiving an embedding with the network whose weights are generated.

Under certain conditions, and allowing the embedding encoder and weight generator to be arbitrarily large, the generated network can be smaller by orders of magnitude. That comparison concerns the function-implementing networks. Separately, for a structured target function, the authors show an orders-of-magnitude reduction in total trainable parameters relative to standard networks and embedding methods.
neurips-2020-on-the-modularity-of-hypern.tldr: Expressivity results identify conditions where hypernetworks represent input-specific functions with substantially smaller networks or fewer total parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies gradient temporal-difference learning with neural networks in an off-policy setting. Its objective is to minimize mean squared Bellman error, a measure of how closely a learned value function satisfies the relationship between current values and subsequent rewards and values. The focus is on establishing an optimization guarantee for this neural learning problem.

The authors reformulate the minimization problem as a min-max optimization involving two over-parameterized neural networks. One plays the primal role and the other the dual role. This paired formulation provides the basis for a neural gradient temporal-difference algorithm, connecting the original Bellman-error objective to an optimization problem that the proposed updates can address.

The convergence analysis considers two-layer networks with ReLU activations and m neurons. It proves that the algorithm computes an approximately optimal solution to the Bellman-error minimization problem as m tends to infinity. The result therefore gives a guarantee in the analyzed large-width regime, linking over-parameterization, the primal-dual formulation, and the behavior of neural temporal-difference learning.
neurips-2020-provably-efficient-neural-g.tldr: A primal-dual neural formulation gives gradient temporal-difference learning an approximate optimality guarantee as two-layer ReLU network width grows without bound.

paragraphs: Explanations of a trained black-box model can vary in quality, while choosing an inherently interpretable model can involve an accuracy trade-off. ExpO combines elements of these approaches by making explanation quality part of training. It regularizes the predictive model so that explanations produced afterward are better supported by the behavior the model has learned.

The proposed regularizers are differentiable, do not depend on a particular model family, and require no domain knowledge to define. These properties make explanation quality an optimization target rather than only a criterion checked after training. The approach retains a distinction between the predictive model and its post-hoc explanation system while deliberately shaping the former to improve the latter.

The authors show improvements in fidelity and stability, two common measures of explanation quality. They also conduct a user study on a realistic task, finding that improvements in those measures lead to significantly more useful explanations. This human evaluation connects the technical criteria to practical usefulness, supporting training-time regularization as a way to improve subsequent interpretation.
neurips-2020-regularizing-black-box-mode.tldr: ExpO trains black-box models with explanation-quality regularizers, improving explanation fidelity, stability, and usefulness in a user study.

paragraphs: Rel3D addresses how systems learn spatial relationships between objects, such as whether a laptop is on a table. The authors identify a shortage of large-scale, high-quality three-dimensional ground truth in existing datasets. They construct a human-annotated dataset that supports studying these relationships and measuring how much three-dimensional information helps predict them.

The central data-collection idea is to create minimally contrastive pairs. Two scenes are almost identical, but a particular spatial relation is true in one and false in the other. This makes the difference relevant to the relationship especially important. The proposed crowdsourcing method uses this pairing to reduce dataset bias and provide more focused examples of what a relation means.

The authors empirically show that these examples can reveal problems in existing relation-detection models and support sample-efficient training. Rel3D therefore serves two connected purposes: evaluating whether models respond to meaningful spatial differences and supplying training examples organized around those differences. Its three-dimensional annotations also enable direct investigation of the value of 3D information on human-labeled data.
neurips-2020-rel3d-a-minimally-contrasti.tldr: Rel3D uses nearly identical 3D scene pairs with different spatial relationships to reduce dataset bias and improve evaluation and training.

paragraphs: Multi-agent learning often assumes that the underlying model is known accurately, even though an agent may lack reliable information about matters such as other agents' rewards. This paper explicitly incorporates model uncertainty into a robust Markov game. The goal is to find policies that remain an equilibrium while accounting for uncertainty in the game model.

The authors introduce a robust Nash equilibrium for this setting: a solution where no agent has an incentive to deviate, with robustness incorporated into the solution concept. They develop a Q-learning algorithm for finding these policies and establish convergence under certain conditions. This provides a theoretical foundation for treating uncertainty as part of strategic learning.

For large state-action spaces, they derive robust multi-agent policy gradients and construct an actor-critic algorithm with function approximation. Experiments cover uncertain cooperative and competitive environments. The proposed algorithm outperforms several baseline multi-agent methods that do not account for model uncertainty, supporting the practical benefit of including that uncertainty in both the problem formulation and learning procedure.
neurips-2020-robust-multi-agent-reinforc.tldr: Robust Markov games support equilibrium learning under model uncertainty, with conditional convergence guarantees and improved empirical multi-agent performance.

paragraphs: SemiNAS addresses the cost of obtaining training data for neural architecture search. A controller needs examples of architectures paired with measured accuracy, but producing those measurements is expensive. Unevaluated architectures are much cheaper to obtain. The method uses them to expand the data available to an accuracy predictor without evaluating every candidate.

It first trains a predictor on a small collection of measured architecture-accuracy pairs. The predictor then assigns estimated accuracies to many unevaluated architectures. These generated pairs are added to the original data to improve the predictor further. The resulting predictor can support different search algorithms by estimating how well their candidates will perform.

On NASBench-101, SemiNAS achieves comparable accuracy to a gradient-based method using one seventh as many measured pairs, and reports higher accuracy than the evaluated baselines when architecture counts are matched. The paper also reports results on ImageNet and on low-resource and robustness settings for LJSpeech text-to-speech. Together, these findings demonstrate both reduced evaluation cost and improved outcomes under the tested resource constraints.
neurips-2020-semi-supervised-neural-arch.tldr: SemiNAS augments measured architecture data with predicted accuracies for unevaluated candidates, improving search efficiency across vision and speech tasks.

paragraphs: SIRI addresses locating a target in a panoramic street-view image from a language description. The task requires connecting mentioned objects with spatial relationship words. The authors argue that explicitly representing object-level relationships and extracting the relevant spatial information are crucial components that existing approaches lack.

The network first correlates visual features at an implicit object level in a projected latent space. It then uses individual spatial relationship words to distill those features, producing different activations for different relationships. Global position priors supply positional information to reduce ambiguity in reasoning about locations across the panorama. Finally, linguistic and visual features are combined to predict the target position.

On Touchdown, the authors report accuracy around 24% better than the state-of-the-art method under an evaluation that counts predictions within an 80-pixel radius. They also report good generalization on an extended dataset collected using the same settings. The findings support explicitly connecting relationship words to visual feature processing and including global position information in language-guided localization.
neurips-2020-siri-spatial-relation-induc.tldr: SIRI uses spatial relationship words to guide visual features and improve language-based target localization in panoramic street views.

paragraphs: Recurrent vision models repeatedly process information, but training them with back-propagation through time uses memory that grows linearly with the number of processing steps. The authors propose that this requirement limits their effectiveness by constraining model design. Larger networks and more extensive recurrent dynamics must compete for the available training memory.

They introduce contractor recurrent back-propagation, or C-RBP, a learning algorithm whose memory complexity remains constant with respect to the number of recurrent steps. This changes the computational constraint on using longer recurrent processing. The contribution concerns memory scaling with processing steps, making expansive recurrent dynamics more accessible within the proposed training framework.

On a synthetic contour-tracing task, C-RBP-trained models detect long-range spatial dependencies that the tested back-propagation-through-time models cannot. On MS-COCO panoptic segmentation, the recurrent models outperform the leading feed-forward approach while using fewer free parameters. These findings support the authors' view that the training algorithm can be an important bottleneck, and they present C-RBP as a general-purpose approach for applications benefiting from recurrent dynamics.
neurips-2020-stable-and-expressive-recur.tldr: C-RBP trains recurrent vision models with memory constant in the number of recurrent steps and shows strong contour-tracing and segmentation results.

paragraphs: Truncated linear regression observes a sample only when its response falls within a specified set. The response still follows a linear relationship plus independent noise, but some outcomes never enter the dataset. This paper studies recovering a high-dimensional coefficient vector when only a small number of its entries are nonzero, combining truncation with sparsity.

The authors analyze stochastic gradient descent for a version of the LASSO objective adapted to truncation. Under favorable conditions on the inputs and noise, the method is computationally and statistically efficient. For an n-dimensional vector with k nonzero entries and m retained samples, it attains optimal Euclidean reconstruction error of order square root of k log n divided by m.

As a consequence, the guarantees yield an efficient, information-theoretically optimal algorithm for compressed sensing with truncation, including truncation that can arise from measurement saturation. The theoretical work handles two challenges together: regularization is needed for high dimensionality, while the objective must account for selective observation. Its analysis extends results that previously handled either low-dimensional truncation or untruncated sparse regression.
neurips-2020-truncated-linear-regression.tldr: A truncation-aware LASSO method efficiently recovers sparse high-dimensional linear models at an optimal error rate under favorable input and noise conditions.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can supply simulated experience for reinforcement learning, but inaccurate predictions can undermine the benefit. This paper focuses on deciding when model-generated data should be trusted. Its theoretical analysis shows that restricting model use to state-action pairs with small model error can reduce the performance gap between simulated and real rollouts.

Masked Model-based Actor-Critic, or M2AC, turns that motivation into a policy optimization algorithm. It optimizes a model-based lower bound on the true value function and uses estimated model uncertainty to decide where the model should contribute. The masking mechanism is intended to keep learning from relying too heavily on predictions in places where the model lacks confidence.

Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks show strong performance even with long model rollouts in very noisy environments, and substantial improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support selective model use as an important ingredient in robust policy improvement. The theoretical condition concerns small actual model error, while the practical algorithm uses uncertainty estimates to guide its selection.
neurips-2020-trust-the-model-when-it-is-.tldr: M2AC uses uncertainty-based masking to select model-generated experience, improving policy learning in the tested noisy continuous-control environments.
